chunks: A number of our companions, from Sahl bin Ziyad, from Ja'far bin Muhammad al-Ash'ari, from Ibn al-Qaddah, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:

The wife of Usman bin Maz'un came to the Prophet (peace be upon him and his family) and said, 'O Messenger of Allah! Usman fasts during the day and prays during the night.' So the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) went out angry, carrying his slippers, until he came to Usman and found him praying. So Usman finished his prayer when he saw the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family). He said to him, 'O Usman! Allah the Exalted did not send me with monasticism, but He sent me with the easy, tolerant Hanifiyyah. I fast and I pray and I touch my wife. So whoever loves my nature, let him follow my Sunnah, and from my Sunnah is marriage.'
ai.seo_question: What did the Prophet say about extreme fasting and monasticism in Islam?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Kafi highlights the Prophet’s rejection of extreme asceticism (Rahbaniyyah) by Usman bin Maz'un, emphasizing that Islam promotes a balanced, natural state (Fitrah) rather than monastic withdrawal. In Shia scholarship, this is often cited to validate marriage and sexual intimacy as acts of worship, contrasting with the Christian monastic tradition, and underscores the Prophet’s personal practice of combining devotion with family life. The narrative illustrates the principle of 'Hanifiyyah al-Sahlah' (the easy, upright way), making marriage a core component of the Sunnah for those who follow the Prophet's nature.
